opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just how people's minds work when they've built something. When you design a defense, you spend weeks or months convincing yourself that it works. You have a mental model of why it should stop attacks, and every experiment you run is, in some sense, shaped by that model. So when you then sit down to attack it, you're attacking it through the same lens you used to build it. The blind spots you had when designing it are exactly the blind spots you have when trying to break it.

There's also an incentive problem that I don't think people like to admit. If you're writing a paper about your defense, you really want it to work. Nobody is consciously cheating, but if you try an attack and it fails, you go "great, the defense works," and you move on. If it succeeds, you go "huh, maybe I set up the attack wrong," and you debug it. That asymmetry adds up. Someone attacking a defense they didn't write has the opposite incentive: every failed attack makes them dig in harder, because they're convinced there's a hole somewhere.

And then there's a skill difference. Building defenses and breaking defenses are different crafts. A lot of defense authors run the standard off-the-shelf attacks, like PGD with the default hyperparameters, see that the attack doesn't succeed, and conclude they're robust. But the standard attacks were designed for undefended models. A defense often works precisely by breaking the assumptions those attacks make, such as making gradients noisy, shattered, or uninformative. So the attack fails, not because the model is robust, but because the attack's tooling no longer applies. Someone who spends their time breaking things knows to ask, "Okay, what is this defense doing that makes my attack fail, and how do I route around it?" That adaptive mindset is the whole game, and it's hard to adopt when you're the one who wants the answer to be "it's secure."

That's why I always tell people that the most valuable thing you can do for your defense is hand it to someone else who wants to break it, and ideally someone who'll be a little bit gleeful when they do.

r001.rationale: The response says developers spend weeks or months convincing themselves their defense works, then attack it through the same lens and retain the same blind spots. It also describes wanting the answer to be that the defense is secure.

r002.rationale: The response describes an incentive asymmetry and says authors want their defense to work, but it does not state that showing their own defense fails yields no publishable result.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a big part of it is just that when you build something, you naturally believe in it. You've spent months on this defense, you have a mental model of why it should work, and that model shapes where you look. You test the things you think an attacker would do, and those happen to be exactly the things your defense was designed to handle. So of course it holds up. The attacks that actually break it are usually ones that come from a direction you didn't think about, and by construction you didn't think about them, so you don't try them.

There's also a real incentive problem. If you're the person who built the thing, finding a break is bad news for you. You're not consciously avoiding it, but when an evaluation gives you an ambiguous result, it's very easy to say, "oh, that's probably a bug in my attack code" rather than "that's probably a bug in my defense." I've seen this so many times. Someone runs an adversarial attack, it doesn't work, and they conclude the defense is robust. But the honest question is: did the attack fail because the defense is good, or because the attack is broken? Most of the time it's the latter. Gradient masking is the classic example. The defense makes the gradients useless, the standard attack flails around, and the authors declare victory. But nothing about the model is actually more robust, you've just broken the tool people use to measure robustness.

And then there's a skill mismatch. Breaking things is a different skill from building things. The way I approach evaluating a defense is almost adversarial toward myself, in the sense that I assume the defense is broken and my job is to figure out how. I'll spend a lot of time looking at the weird edge cases, trying attacks that seem like they shouldn't work, loosening the threat model and tightening it back up, just to understand what the defense is actually doing versus what the paper claims it's doing. That mindset is kind of unnatural if you're the one who wants the thing to succeed. So I think the practical answer is that you really need someone else, ideally someone who has no stake in the outcome and who has broken a lot of defenses before, to try to break yours. Or at the very least, you have to be willing to be your own worst enemy for a while, and most people, understandably, aren't.

r001.rationale: It says developers naturally believe in a defense they have invested months in, and that wanting it to succeed makes a break-seeking mindset unnatural.

r002.rationale: It describes finding a break as bad news and an incentive problem, but does not mention that showing one’s own defense fails yields no publishable result.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is that, when you build a defense, you have a particular model in your head of how an attack is going to work. And you build something that addresses that. Then, when you go to evaluate it, you tend to attack it in ways that are consistent with the model you had when you designed it. It’s very hard to step outside of that and ask, “What assumption am I making here that I could violate?”

There’s also a difference in incentives. If I’ve spent months developing a defense, finding an attack against it means discovering that the thing I’ve been working on doesn’t work. If I’m coming in from the outside specifically to break it, finding that same attack is success. You don’t have to be dishonest for that difference to affect how you approach the problem or how long you keep looking.

That’s why independent evaluation is so useful. Someone else brings a different set of assumptions, and the thing you never thought to test might be the first thing they try.

r001.rationale: The response says developers who have spent months on a defense may find it hard to approach testing as an outsider trying to break it, because an attack shows their work does not succeed.

r002.rationale: It describes the disincentive of discovering that one’s defense does not work, but does not mention a lack of a publishable result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think when you build a defense, you have some particular attacks in mind. You understand how those attacks work, and you design something that stops them. And then, when you go to evaluate it, you tend to keep thinking in that same way. It’s hard to step back and ask, “What if the attacker does something completely different?”

There’s also a difference in incentives. As a defender, you want the thing you built to work. As an attacker, I come in with no attachment to how it’s supposed to work. I just need to find one way around it. That doesn’t mean the defense developers aren’t capable of finding attacks. But having somebody independent try to break it is really valuable, because they’re not carrying around the same assumptions you made when you built it.

r001.rationale: The response says defenders want the defense they built to work and contrasts that with an attacker who has no attachment and seeks a way around it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses incentives generally but does not mention that finding no attack or showing the defense fails offers no publishable result.
